coredata.dc:description: Imidazolium-based ionic liquids and imidazolium-based organic–inorganic hybrid alkaline anion exchange membranes (AEMs) are synthesized and investigated in the present work. The imidazolium-based hybrid AEMs are prepared via in situ cross-linking of styrene, acrylonitrile, 1-vinyl-propyl-triethoxysilaneimidazolium chloride ([VPSIm][Cl]) and 1-vinyl-3-butylimidazolium bromide ([VBIm][Br]), followed by anion exchange with hydroxide ions. The water uptake and swelling degree of the hybrid AEMs decrease with increasing [VPSIm][Cl] content due to the formation of an Si–O–Si inorganic network in the membranes. The resulting organic–inorganic hybrid AEMs show good thermal stability, excellent mechanical properties and high conductivity (above 10−2 Scm−1 at room temperature in liquid water). Compared with samples without the addition of [VPSIm][Cl], the hybrid membranes show much higher alkaline stability, and the hybrid AEMs displayed excellent chemical stability up to 480h in 2M KOH solution at 60°C.

ce:abstract-sec.ce:simple-para: Imidazolium-based ionic liquids and imidazolium-based organic–inorganic hybrid alkaline anion exchange membranes (AEMs) are synthesized and investigated in the present work. The imidazolium-based hybrid AEMs are prepared via in situ cross-linking of styrene, acrylonitrile, 1-vinyl-propyl-triethoxysilaneimidazolium chloride ([VPSIm][Cl]) and 1-vinyl-3-butylimidazolium bromide ([VBIm][Br]), followed by anion exchange with hydroxide ions. The water uptake and swelling degree of the hybrid AEMs decrease with increasing [VPSIm][Cl] content due to the formation of an Si–O–Si inorganic network in the membranes. The resulting organic–inorganic hybrid AEMs show good thermal stability, excellent mechanical properties and high conductivity (above 10−2 Scm−1 at room temperature in liquid water). Compared with samples without the addition of [VPSIm][Cl], the hybrid membranes show much higher alkaline stability, and the hybrid AEMs displayed excellent chemical stability up to 480h in 2M KOH solution at 60°C.

ce:section.ce:para: With the increasing demand for clean and efficient energy worldwide, fuel cell as an environmentally friendly power source and substitute for conventional fossil fuel processes, are attracting more and more attention [1]. Among several types of fuel cells, polymer electrolyte fuel cells using proton exchange membranes (PEMs) and alkaline anion exchange membranes (AEMs) as solid electrolytes, are being considered as renewable and portable energy devices due to their high energy conversion efficiency, environmental friendliness, and their flexibility for use in various kinds of electric vehicles [2,3]. In the past decades, much effort has been devoted to developing PEMs for proton exchange membrane fuel cell (PEMFC) applications. Perfluorosulfonic acid membranes, represented by Nafion as the archetype, are most commonly used in PEMFCs due to their high proton conductivity and excellent chemical stability in acidic conditions. However, the exhaustible precious metal electrocatalysts required in PEMs (such as platinum) and the high cost of Nafion membranes are hindering the widespread commercialization of PEMFCs.

Replacing PEMs with AEMs is a solution to the problem of cost, in principle, because the use of abundant transition metal electrocatalysts (such as Ni, Co and Fe) is feasible in anion exchange membrane fuel cells (AEMFCs) with high pH AEMs as electrolytes [4–6]. Furthermore, AEMFCs offer fuel flexibility, reduced fuel crossover, and enhanced reaction kinetics that may make these devices desirable in certain applications [7,8]. Therefore, AEMs and AEMFC have attracted much attention in recent years. However, meeting the comprehensive requirements of high hydroxide anion conductivity, robust mechanical properties and good chemical stability in alkaline environment, not to mention robust device performance, is a key challenge for the application of AEMs in AEMFCs [9].

Recently, much research effort has been spent on developing high-performance AEM materials with quaternary ammonium cationic groups based on polysulfone [10], poly(arylene ether sulfone) [11–17], poly(arylene ether ketone) [18,19], poly(phenylene oxide) [20,21] poly(fluorenyl ether ketone sulfone) [22,23] and polypropylene [24]. It should be pointed out that the practical application of AEMs is strongly limited by their alkaline stability and mechanical properties. A growing effort is underway to develop AEM materials that simultaneously possess high hydroxide conductivity, good mechanical properties, and robust alkaline stability under the operating conditions of AEMFCs [25–37]. However, most of these membranes were unstable in alkaline media especially at temperatures above 60°C and at high KOH concentrations (above 1M). Therefore, developing AEMs with high alkaline stability is still an urgent issue [38,39].

Most AEMs that have been reported were prepared by solution casting, and the treatment of hazardous organic solvents is a problem for large-scale production of membranes. Chemical cross-linking is a common but effective method for the preparation of AEMs, which could both suppress the water swelling and improve the mechanical strength of AEMs [40]. Beside quaternary ammonium cationic groups, guanidinium [41], phosphonium [42], benzimidazolium [43], metal-cation [44] and imidazolium [45–50] based AEMs have been investigated. Imidazolium-based ionic liquids (ILs) are mostly room-temperature organic salts, have attracted much attention as electrolytes for various processes due to their excellent thermal stability, low volatility and high conductivity. The AEMs with imidazolium cations showed better stability in alkaline solution at elevated temperature compared with AEMs containing quaternary ammonium cationic groups [50]. However, the mechanical strength of AEMs must be enhanced.

In this paper, we propose a new type of cross-linked alkaline hybrid AEM based on imidazolium-based ILs, [VBIm][Br] (1-vinyl-3-butylimidazolium bromide) and [VPSIm][Cl] (1-vinyl-propyl-triethoxysilaneimidazolium chloride). In this investigation, [VPSIm][Cl] acts both as a monomer and cross-linker which resulted in the formation of an Si–O–Si inorganic network in the membranes. An Si–O–Si inorganic network phase was chosen because it can effectively resist water swelling of the AEMs, thus assuring good mechanical strength and lowering fuel crossover. Zhang [51] and Xu [52] have fabricated polysilsesquioxane-based AEMs and PPO/SiO2 hybrid AEMs with Si–O–Si inorganic network phase, respectively, and the membranes showed good alkaline stability and suitable for potential AEMFC applications. In the present work, it is expected that the cross-linked alkaline hybrid membrane will offer good mechanical strength, high hydroxide ion conductivity and excellent alkaline stability. The properties of the membranes, such as water uptake, swelling degree, ion exchange capability (IEC), hydroxide ion conductivity, thermal stability, mechanical properties and chemical stability in high pH solution were investigated.

Styrene, acrylonitrile, N-vinylimidazole, N-butylbromide, ethylether, 3-chloropropyltriethoxysilane, pure para divinylbenzene (DVB), benzoin ethylether, ethyl acetate, tetraethyl orthosilicate (TEOS), potassium hydroxide, and sodium hydroxide were used as purchased. All of the vinyl monomers were made inhibitor-free by passing the liquid through a column filled with basic Al2O3 to remove the polymerization inhibitor. Distilled deionized water was used for all experiments.

[VBIm][Br] was synthesized as shown in Scheme 1. N-vinylimidazole (9.41g, 0.1mol) and an equivalent molar amount of n-butylbromide (13.7g, 0.1mol) were added into a 100mL round bottomed flask equipped with a mechanical stirrer and a nitrogen inlet/outlet. The mixture was stirred at room temperature under nitrogen atmosphere for 48h. The resultant viscous oil was washed with ethyl acetate three times, and dried in dynamic vacuum at 80°C for 24h before use. [VBIm][Br] was obtained as a yellow transparent viscous oil (17.10g, 74% yield). 1H NMR (400MHz, DMSO) δ 9.47 (s, 1H, N–CH–N), 8.19 (s, 1H, N–CH=C), 7.93 (s, 1H, C=CH–N), 7.28 (dd, J=15.6, 8.7Hz, 1H, N–CH=C), 5.95 (dd, J=15.6, 2.3Hz, 1H, C=HCH), 5.43 (dd, J=8.7, 2.3Hz, 1H, C=HCH), 4.20 (t, J=7.2Hz, 2H, N–CH2–C), 2.10 −1.65 (m, 2H, C–CH2–C), 1.55–1.12 (m, 2H, C–CH2–C), 0.92 (t, J=7.4Hz, 3H, C–CH3).

As shown in Scheme 1, [VPSIm][Cl] was synthesized similar to [VBIm][Br]. N-vinylimidazole (9.41g, 0.1mol), an equivalent molar amount of 3-chloropropyltriethoxysilane (24.80g, 0.1mol), and benzoquinone (0.171g, 0.5wt% of the monomer) were added to a 100mL round bottomed flask equipped with a mechanical stirrer and a nitrogen inlet/outlet. The mixture was stirred at 65°C under nitrogen atmosphere for 48h. The resultant viscous oil was washed with ethylether three times and then dried under dynamic vacuum at 80°C for 24h before use. [VPSIm][Cl] was obtained as a yellow transparent viscous liquid (25.31g, 76% yield).1H NMR (400MHz, DMSO): δ 9.64 (s, 1H, N–CH–N), 7.93 (s, 1H, N–CH=C), 7.59 (s, 1H, C=CH–N), 7.17 (dd, J=15.8, 8.9Hz, 1H, N–CH–C), 5.48 (dd, J=15.9, 1.1Hz, 1H, C=HCH), 4.85 (dd, J=8.9, 1.0Hz, 1H, C=HCH), 4.16 (t, J=7.2Hz, 2H, N–CH2–C), 3.77–3.68 (m, 6H, O–CH2–C), 1.96–1.77 (m, 2H, C–CH2–C), 1.17–1.08 (m, 9H, C–CH3), 0.59–0.49 (m, 2H, C–CH2–Si).

A mixture of styrene/acrylonitrile (1:3 weight ratio), [VBIm][Br] (33.3wt%), [VPSIm][Cl] (0–25wt%), divinylbenzene (2wt%, based on the weight of monomer), and 1wt% of benzoin isobutyl ether was added into a glass bottle. The mixture was stirred and ultrasonicated to obtain a homogeneous solution. The resultant mixture was then cast into a glass mold and photo-cross-linked by irradiation with 250nm UV light 30min. The resultant IL-based membranes were immersed in TEOS at room temperature for 2h, and then immersed in N2-saturated 2M KOH solution at 60°C for 24h. The converted membranes then were immersed in N2-saturated deionized water and washed with deionized water until the pH of residual water was neutral.

1H NMR spectra were recorded on a AVANCE III 400MHz spectrometer. Fourier transform infrared (FT-IR) spectra of the polymers were recorded on a Nicolet Avatar 370 spectrometer in the range of 4000–400cm−1. Thermal analysis was carried out by Netzsch 209 F3 thermogravimetric analyzer (TGA), and samples were heated from 30°C to 650°C at a heating rate of 10°Cmin−1 under nitrogen flow. The tensile properties of the membranes were measured using an Instron Model 5KN/WDT-5 device at 25°C at a crosshead speed of 5mmmin− 1.

The resistance of the membrane samples was measured over the frequency range from 0.1Hz to 1MHz by four-point probe alternating current (AC) impedance spectroscopy, using an electrode system connected with an electrochemical workstation (Zahner IM6 EX). All the samples were fully hydrated in N2-saturated deionized water for at least 24h prior to the conductivity measurement. Conductivity measurements under fully hydrated conditions were conducted in a chamber filled with N2-saturated deionized water. All the samples were equilibrated for at least 30min at a given temperature. Repeated measurements were obtained at 10-min intervals, until no change in conductivity was observed. ce:section.ce:section-title: Preparation of alkaline hybrid anion exchange membranes
ce:section.ce:para: The imidazolium-based organic–inorganic hybrid alkaline AEMs were synthesized as shown in Scheme 2. A homogeneous solution containing [VBIm][Br], styrene/acrylonitrile, [VPSIm][Cl] (5–25wt %), and DVB was photo-cross-linked by irradiation with UV light. The resultant copolymer membranes were immersed in TEOS at room temperature for 2h, the excess TEOS on the surface was eliminated by washing with water, and then immersed in N2-saturated 1M KOH solution at 60°C for 24h to convert the membrane from Br− and Cl− to OH− form. The produced membranes are denoted as Membrane-x, the subscript x indicates the weight ratio of [VPSIm][Cl] in the membrane. All the membranes are transparent and flexible as shown in Fig. 1.

The chemical structure of imidazolium-based organic–inorganic hybrid alkaline AEMs was confirmed by FT-IR spectroscopy measurements. Fig. 2 shows the FT-IR spectra of Membrane-x samples. For all the membrane samples, the broad absorption band at approximately 3348 and 2230cm−1 can be attributed to the stretching vibrations of –OH and –C≡N groups, respectively. The absorption bands appearing at 2930cm−1 are assigned to the stretching vibrations of methylene and methyl. The peaks at 1450–1600cm−1 confirm the existence of the benzene ring. Absorption bands at 1582cm−1 and 700cm−1 arise from the vibrational mode of the imidazolium cations. The absorption bands at 1125cm−1 were observed due to Si–O–Si stretching. The content of the Si–O–Si network increases with increasing [VPSIm][Cl] form Membrane-5 to Membrane-25. This trend was confirmed by a gradual increase in the intensity of Si–O–Si stretching absorption at 1125cm−1.

ce:section.ce:section-title: IEC, water uptake and swelling degree
ce:section.ce:para: The water uptake of AEMs is strongly related to their conductivity and mechanical properties. The absorbed water can facilitate the transport of ions to maintain high ionic conductivity of the materials. However, excessive water absorption may lead to the deterioration of the AEMs’ mechanical properties. An ideal AEM should exhibit proper water uptake, high conductivity, and excellent mechanical properties. Table 1 summarizes the water uptake, swelling degree, IEC values and conductivity of the AEMs. As listed in Table 1, the water uptake of the membranes decreased upon increasing content of [VPSIm][Cl] because of the formation of the Si–O–Si network in the hybrid membranes. The water uptake for Membrane-0 is approximately 206%, while Membrane-25 shows a much lower water uptake of 137%. Compared with the PSANx-[DAMIm][OH]y membranes in our previous paper [53], the hybrid membranes shows much higher water uptake resulted by the much more ionic liquid content in the hybrid membranes. Swelling degree is also an important parameter in determining the performance of the membranes. As expected, the swelling degree of the hybrid membranes decreased with an increasing [VPSIm][Cl] content, with values of 55%, 49%, 47%, 43%, 42% and 39%, respectively, as shown in Table 1. The IEC value determines, in part, the water uptake, swelling degree and conductivity of the AEMs. In the present work, AEMs with different IECs were prepared by adjusting the ratio of [VPSIm][Cl] in the membranes, and the IEC values of the hybrid AEMs obtained by titration are listed in Table 1. The ionizable groups of the composite membranes were provided by imidazolium-based ionic liquids and it is not surprising that the titrated IEC values of the membranes increased from 1.58 to 2.56meqg−1 upon increasing the [VPSIm][Cl] content from 0 to 25wt%. In general, the higher IEC values, the higher water uptake and swelling degree. However, in the present work, when the content of [VPSIm][Cl] increased from 0% to 25% in the membranes, the water uptake decreased from 206% to 137%, and swelling degree decreased from 55% to 39%. This phenomenon was observed because of the formation of the Si–O–Si inorganic network in the hybrid membranes which results in less water uptake.

The thermal stability of the membrane samples was evaluated using TGA under a nitrogen flow at a heating rate of 10°Cmin−1 from room temperature to 650°C. Fig. 3 shows typical TGA curves of the hybrid membranes containing a range of [VPSIm][Cl] contents. All of the membranes showed a similar degradation tendency. Four consecutive mass loss steps can be seen in the TGA thermograms. The first weight loss stage of less than 7% occurred from room temperature to 200°C, which was induced by the evaporation of absorbed water from the sample. The second weight loss stage appeared from 200°C to 300°C, and could be attributed to the thermal degradation of nitrile and phenyl groups on the side chain of copolymer. The third degradation from 300 to 400 is ascribed to the decomposition of copolymer's imidazole groups. The fourth weight loss stage occurred above 550°C and was caused by the decomposition of the polymer's backbone. Compared with Membrane-0 without [VPSIm][Cl], the composite membranes absorbed less water, and had less weight loss above 400°C due to the formation of the Si–O–Si inorganic network in the hybrid membranes. All the membranes exhibited weight losses of less than 7% below 200°C, confirming the good thermal stability of the composite membranes, far beyond the range of AEMFC applications.

The mechanical properties of the Membrane-0 and hybrid membranes were measured using a universal testing machine with a crosshead speed of 5mmmin−1 at room temperature. The measured tensile strength, tensile modulus and elongation at break values are collected in Table 2. The tensile strength of all the membranes was in the range of 11.7–28.0MPa, with a tensile modulus of 256–959MPa, and elongation at break values of 6.4–14.5%. Compared with Membrane-0 without [VPSIm][Cl], the hybrid membranes showed higher tensile strength and tensile modulus but lower elongation at break due to the formation of the Si–O–Si inorganic network in the hybrid membranes. When the content of [VPSIm][Cl] was increased from 5wt% to 25wt%, the tensile modulus and tensile strength of the membranes was increased from 393.6MPa and 13.3MPa to 959.3MPa and 28.0MPa, respectively, which significantly increased the membrane mechanical properties.

The performance of a fuel cell usually depends on the AEM's conductivity. The effect of the [VPSIm][Cl] content on the ionic conductivity of AEMs was also studied in the present work, and the ion conductivities of hybrid membranes with various [VPSIm][Cl] contents were measured. Fig. 4 shows the temperature dependence of the conductivity of Membrane-0 and the hybrid membranes. As expected, the conductivity increased as the temperature increased for all AEMs. This phenomenon is mainly due to the faster migration of ions and higher diffusivity of water and ions with increasing temperature. Furthermore, the polymer matrix will be more flexible and more water will be absorbed by the AEMs at a higher temperature, which results in a more swollen membrane structure and wider ion-conducting channels, leading to a higher conductivity. It can be clearly seen that the conductivities of the hybrid AEMs increased with the introduction of [VPSIm][Cl] at first. For instance, the conductivity of Membrane-0 is 3.58×10−2 Scm−1 at 30°C, while Membrane-5 showed a conductivity of 4.10×10−2 Scm−1 under the same conditions. This increase is because of more ionizable groups resulting from the introduction of [VPSIm][Cl] in the hybrid membrane. However, the excess introduction of [VPSIm][Cl] can result in a decrease of the conductivity. This is probably due to the formation of the Si–O–Si inorganic network in the hybrid membranes that can impede ion transport. Though the IEC values increase with increasing [VPSIm][Cl] content in the hybrid membranes, the formation of Si–O–Si inorganic network results in less water uptake and lower swelling degree which lead to a lower conductivity. Among all the samples, Membrane-5 shows the highest hydroxide ion conductivity of 9.05×10−2 Scm−1 at 90°C which is a desirable value for operation of a membrane in an AEMFC.

where b is the slope of the regressed linear ln(σ) vs 1000/T plots, and R is the gas constant (8.314J(molK)−1). The E a obtained from the slope of the line is also presented in Fig. 5, and ranged from 10.44 to 12.17kJmol−1. It can be seen that the E a values are strongly related to the IEC values. The content of ionizable groups increased with the increasing content [VPSIm][Cl] in the hybrid AEMs, while a reverse order was observed for the activation energy. This phenomenon also can be found in other ionic liqiud based AEMs reported by the previous papers [45,50]. The E a values of all the hybrid membranes were lower than that of Membrane-0 without [VPSIm][Cl], showing that proton transfer needs less energy in the hybrid membrane due to the more ionizable groups resulting from the addition of [VPSIm][Cl].

The chemical stability of alkaline anion exchange membranes is recognized as a key factor that affects their performance in devices, especially at high pH and elevated temperatures. The long-term stability of membranes was evaluated by immersing the membrane samples in 2M KOH aqueous solution at 60°C and 80°C for various times. The changes in hydroxide ion conductivity of the tested membranes were measured after the free KOH on the surface of membranes was rinsed with water. Fig. 6 shows the conductivity of Membrane-0 without [VPSIm][Cl] and other hybrid membranes after treatment with 2M KOH solution at 60°C (A) and 80°C (B). The Membrane-0 showed an initial conductivity of 3.58×10−2 Scm−1, however, its conductivity decreased gradually with time, and the membrane was broken into pieces after 15 and 12 days for 60°C and 80°C respectively. Degradations of the hybrid membranes can be observed in high temperature, and propably follow the ring-opening degradation mechanism which proposed by Yan and Henkensmeier [39,54]. It is worth noting that all the hybrid membranes retained approximately 80% of their initial conductivity after being treated in a 2M KOH solution at 80°C for 12 days and at 60°C for 20 days. All the hybrid membranes retained their shape and flexibility during the alkaline stability test time in KOH solution. The IEC values of the membranes showed a similar trend as the conductivity before and after the test, and there was no obviously weight loss (less than 5wt%) can be observed after being treated in a 2M KOH solution at 60°C for 20 days (Membrane-0 broke into pieces), which further confirms the excellent alkaline stability of the hybrid membranes at 60°C, but it declined at 80°C in 2M KOH solution. Organic-inorganic hybrid AEMs with an Si–O–Si network are reasonably stable under alkaline condition as was observed in previous reports [51,52]. Besides, it has been reported that an electrode containing a Si–O–Si inorganic network structure can function properly in alkaline condition [55], and the hydroxide ions can induce Si–O–Si rearrangement in the inorganic network structure, which ensures that the structure of polymer is not destroyed [56]. It is assumed that the alkaline stability of hybrid membranes was enhanced probably due to the robust structure formed in the hybrid membranes which protected the imidazolium cations against the hydroxide attack [57].

A series of hybrid anion exchange membranes with different [VPSIm][Cl] contents were designed and prepared through irradiation with ultraviolet light. The resultant hybrid membranes had good thermal stability and mechanical properties. The water uptake and swelling degree of the hybrid membranes decreased with an increase in the [VPSIm][Cl] content due to the formation of an Si–O–Si inorganic network in the membranes. The conductivity of the hybrid membranes increased with the initial introduction of [VPSIm][Cl] due to the higher IEC values of the resulting materials, however, the conductivity decreased with a further excess addition of [VPSIm][Cl] due to the lower water uptake of the membranes with too much Si–O–Si network formation. All the membranes showed conductivity up to approximately 1×10−2 Scm−1, and Membrane-5 showed a conductivity of 4.10×10−2 Scm−1 at 30°C. Compared with Membrane-0 without [VPSIm][Cl], it is worth noting that the hybrid membranes showed a higher alkaline stability probably due to the reinforcing structure formed in the hybrid membranes which resulted from the Si–O–Si inorganic network.
